intro: BEHR Premium 1-Part Epoxy is the best concrete floor paint for most homes: an epoxy-fortified acrylic that rolls on like ordinary latex, is labeled for interior and exterior concrete, and tints to a wide range of colors. With good prep, a one-part floor paint like it commonly lasts three to five years in a garage and longer in a basement.

Every pick on this page is a one-part product: open, stir and roll, with no hardener and no pot life. That makes paint the right tool for floors that carry feet, furniture and the occasional mower, and the wrong one for a slab where a car parks every night. Below are six paints matched to the rooms they suit, then the checks, prep steps and coverage math that decide whether the paint stays on.
quickAnswer: Start with BEHR Premium 1-Part Epoxy for garages, basements and patios. Pick Rust-Oleum EpoxyShield 1-Part for a glossier garage floor, Sherwin-Williams Tread-Plex for shops and utility rooms, Benjamin Moore Floor and Patio for living spaces and porches, and INSL-X Sure Step or KILZ Over Armor where traction or a rough slab is the problem. For daily parking, use a two-part coating instead.

blocks.p: If you are unsure, buy BEHR. It handles the widest range of floors with the fewest trade-offs. Move to Rust-Oleum for more shine in a garage, Tread-Plex when boots and carts are the daily load, and Benjamin Moore when the floor is part of a living space.

Sure Step and Over Armor are specialists. Use them only where poor traction or a rough, patched slab is the real problem, and smooth paint everywhere else. Our ranking of the [best epoxy garage floor coatings](/best-garage-floor-epoxy/) is the next step up if a car parks on the floor every day.

sections.h: The 6 Best Concrete Floor Paints in 2026, Ranked

blocks.p: The ranking draws on what each manufacturer publishes (resin type, coverage, recoat and cure windows, approved surfaces), on warranty terms and on patterns that repeat in owner feedback. None of these paints was put through lab or wear trials by us; where a claim rests on a label, the text says so.

blocks.h3: Best Overall: BEHR Premium 1-Part Epoxy Concrete and Garage Floor Paint

blocks.p: BEHR's floor paint takes the top spot because one can covers the most situations. It is a water-based acrylic reinforced with epoxy resin, so it handles like latex: stir, cut in the edges, roll, and rinse the roller in the sink. The label covers interior and exterior concrete, so the same product can do a garage, a basement and a back patio. It dries to a satin finish and tints to dozens of colors at Home Depot, and it works with BEHR's decorative flakes for a speckled look. Owners who prep well commonly describe a hard, even film that mops clean. When complaints show up, they usually trace back to cars parked too early or a glossy slab that was never etched. Plan on two coats and the full vehicle cure on the label.
**Pros:** interior and exterior rating, tints widely, no mixing, water cleanup, accepts decorative flakes.
**Cons:** can lift under hot tires if the cure is rushed; smooth slabs need etching first.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=BEHR+Premium+1-Part+Epoxy+Concrete+Garage+Floor+Paint&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best for Garages: Rust-Oleum EpoxyShield 1-Part Concrete Floor Paint

blocks.p: This is Rust-Oleum's one-can answer for owners who want a coated look without the two-part kit. It is an acrylic floor paint with added epoxy for hardness, and the brand pitches it for resistance to hot-tire pickup, oil and road salt within the limits of a one-part chemistry. The semi-gloss finish looks cleaner and more reflective than satin paints and lets dirt mop or hose off easily, though it also shows dust and footprints more. Colors are limited to a handful of grays and tans plus accents. Rust-Oleum sells a matching etch and degreaser, so you can buy the whole system from one shelf. Owner feedback praises the look and hardness, with the usual warning: floors driven on before full cure, or painted over a sealer, peel first in the tire paths.
**Pros:** garage-focused formula, easy-clean semi-gloss, widely stocked, low odor, matching prep products.
**Cons:** few colors, glossier finish shows dust.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Rust-Oleum+EpoxyShield+1-Part+Concrete+Floor+Paint&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Pro-Grade Paint: Sherwin-Williams ArmorSeal Tread-Plex

blocks.p: Tread-Plex belongs to the ArmorSeal family in Sherwin-Williams' industrial line, which is why it turns up in school corridors and warehouse walkways rather than on big-box shelves. It is a one-component, water-based acrylic that rolls on like paint but is built for heavier foot traffic and frequent cleaning. Its data sheet lists fast dry and recoat times, so two coats in a day is realistic in mild, breezy weather. It tints to many colors including safety yellows for marking walkways and steps. The catches are price per gallon, which runs above retail floor paints, and access, since you buy it at a Sherwin-Williams store. For a workshop, laundry or basement utility room that sees boots and carts, the premium is easy to justify.
**Pros:** commercial-grade acrylic, quick recoat, low VOC, safety colors, knowledgeable store staff.
**Cons:** costs more per gallon, sold mainly through Sherwin-Williams stores.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Sherwin-Williams+ArmorSeal+Tread-Plex&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best for Patios and Porches: Benjamin Moore Floor and Patio Latex Enamel

blocks.p: When the finished look matters as much as toughness, this is the paint. It is an acrylic latex floor enamel for concrete and wood, inside or out, and it tints to almost any color in the Benjamin Moore system, handy for matching trim, siding or a finished basement. It levels to a refined low-luster finish that hides footprints and scuffs better than glossy garage paints, and it has good mildew resistance outdoors. Benjamin Moore does not position it for vehicle traffic, so keep it to patios, porches, sunrooms, mudrooms and basement living areas. Dealer staff can recommend a primer for bare or previously painted concrete. Owners generally report good outdoor color retention when the slab was clean and dry first.
**Pros:** concrete and wood, inside and out; full color matching; low-luster finish hides wear; easy to mop.
**Cons:** not for garage floors with cars, premium price for a latex floor paint.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Benjamin+Moore+Floor+and+Patio+Latex+Enamel&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Slip Resistance: INSL-X Sure Step Acrylic Anti-Slip Coating

blocks.p: INSL-X, part of the Benjamin Moore family, built Sure Step for one job: stopping slips on surfaces that get wet. The grit is suspended in the coating, so the texture goes on with the roller instead of being broadcast by hand, which avoids the bald patches you get when grit settles out of homemade mixes. It is rated for concrete, wood, metal and properly primed surfaces, so one product can unify a run of steps, landings and ramps. Expect a coarse feel underfoot, a spread rate well below smooth floor paint and the need for a roller made for textured coatings. Cleaning takes a stiff brush rather than a mop. On basement stairs, garage entry steps, pool decks and ramps, owners commonly cite the grip as the reason they bought it.
**Pros:** aggregate pre-mixed, multi-surface rating, strong wet traction, water-based and low odor.
**Cons:** coarse texture is harder to clean, lower coverage, limited colors.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=INSL-X+Sure+Step+Anti-Slip+Coating&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best for Worn Concrete: KILZ Over Armor Textured Coating

blocks.p: Over Armor is a heavy, textured acrylic coating rather than a thin paint, and KILZ markets it for weathered wood decks as well as outdoor concrete. Because the film goes on thick, it fills small pits, hairline cracks and patchy repairs that a smooth paint would only outline. The grit also grips better when wet, a real plus on steps, walks and pool surrounds. That thickness costs coverage: the label lists a much lower spread rate than standard floor paint, so buy more cans than you expect. The texture holds dirt and needs a stiff broom or hose. Owners who use it on patios and steps tend to like the look and grip; those who put it on garage floors are less pleased. Keep it outdoors on foot-traffic surfaces.
**Pros:** hides cracks and wear, built-in traction, works on concrete and wood, water cleanup.
**Cons:** low coverage per gallon, texture traps dirt, not for vehicles.

sections.h: Is Floor Paint or a Two-Part Coating Better for Concrete?

blocks.p: Paint is better for floors that carry feet and furniture. A two-part coating is better for floors that carry a parked car every day.

One-part paint dries as its water evaporates and the binder fuses into a film, commonly about 2 to 4 mils dry per coat. A two-part epoxy or polyaspartic cures by a chemical reaction and builds 10 mils or more, with full broadcast floors far thicker. Thin film is why paint is easy, cheap and simple to touch up, and also why it wears through in traffic lanes and lifts where warm tires sit.

blocks.h3: What rolls across the floor decides it

blocks.p: Feet, furniture, a workbench and the occasional lawn mower are well within what paint handles. Basement rec rooms, laundry rooms, covered patios and storage garages are good paint jobs. A daily car, truck or loaded cart is two-part territory. The [best concrete floor coating](/best-concrete-floor-coating/) guide covers epoxy, polyaspartic and hybrid systems for those floors.

blocks.h3: Epoxy on the label does not make it a coating

blocks.p: Epoxy-modified acrylics like BEHR and Rust-Oleum's one-part paints are harder than plain latex, but they are still one-part paint. Expecting garage-kit performance because the can says epoxy is the most common reason behind disappointed reviews.

sections.h: What Types of Concrete Floor Paint Are There?

blocks.p: There are four practical families. Store shelves group floor paint by brand, so knowing which family a can belongs to tells you more than its front label.
Water-based, low odor, tints to anything and stays slightly flexible, which helps outdoor slabs ride out temperature swings. It is the softest family, so furniture legs and doorways wear first.
Still one-part and water-based, but harder and more stain resistant. It is the most popular garage paint family and usually needs a longer cure before vehicles.
Dries hard and levels well, but strong odor, slow drying, yellowing indoors and poor tolerance of alkaline concrete have pushed it aside. Use it only to match an existing oil-based floor.
Grit or a thick body in the can trades an easy-clean surface for traction and the ability to disguise a rough slab.

sections.h: Will Paint Stick to Your Concrete Floor?

blocks.p: It will if the surface is open, dry and rough enough. Three quick checks tell you which of those you have, and skipping them explains most painted floors that peel within a year.

blocks.h3: The water drop test: is something sealing the surface?

blocks.p: Sprinkle water in several spots, middle and edges. If the concrete darkens and absorbs it within about a minute, the surface is open. If it beads, a sealer, curing compound, wax or old coating is present, and paint would bond to that layer instead of the concrete. Strip or grind it first.

blocks.h3: The plastic sheet test: is moisture rising?

blocks.p: Tape an 18-by-18-inch square of clear plastic to the floor with all edges sealed and leave it at least 16 hours, the period ASTM D4263 specifies; a full day is better. Droplets or darker concrete underneath mean vapor is coming through, and paint will blister. This matters most on basement slabs; see our guide to [basement waterproofing systems](/best-basement-waterproofing-systems/) before painting a damp floor.

blocks.h3: The touch and tape test: is it rough enough?

blocks.p: A paint-ready surface feels like 120 to 150 grit sandpaper. A glassy, power-troweled slab needs an etch or light grind. On an old painted floor, press duct tape down hard and rip it off; any paint that lifts must come off before you repaint.

sections.h: How Do You Prep and Paint a Concrete Floor?

blocks.p: Clear, degrease, profile, patch, vacuum and dry, then roll two thin coats on a mild day. The prep takes longer than the painting; budget a full day for a two-car garage and half a day for a basement room.

Empty the room, scrape off drywall mud and old drips, sweep, then scrub oil spots with a concrete degreaser until water stops beading there. For old, deep stains, our guide on [how to get oil out of concrete](/how-to-get-oil-out-of-concrete/) explains poultices and stronger cleaners.

Most house slabs take a citric or diluted muriatic acid etch: wet the floor, spread the etch, scrub, watch for light fizzing, then rinse at least twice. Very smooth or hard slabs respond better to a rented diamond grinder, which also removes thin old coatings.

Fill cracks with a paintable concrete patch, let it cure, then vacuum the whole floor; etch dust is a hidden bond-breaker. Let the slab dry 24 to 48 hours after washing, longer in a cool basement. New concrete needs at least 28 days of cure before any paint.

Apply when air and slab are roughly 50 to 90 degrees Fahrenheit and the slab is at least 5 degrees above the dew point. Prime if the label calls for it, cut in the edges a few feet at a time, then roll with a 3/8 to 1/2-inch nap in 4-by-6-foot sections, keeping a wet edge. Two thin coats always beat one heavy one, and respect the recoat window on the can.

sections.h: How Much Concrete Floor Paint Do You Need?

blocks.p: A two-car garage takes roughly 3 gallons for two coats of a smooth floor paint. Smooth paints commonly list about 300 to 400 square feet per gallon per coat on dense concrete, and less on porous or freshly etched slabs where the first coat soaks in. Textured coatings often cover a quarter to a third of that.

blocks.h3: Plan from the can, not a rule of thumb

blocks.p: Always work from the spread rate printed on your product, and add a margin for a thirsty first coat.
Buy every can in one trip, and for tinted paint, box the cans together before you start. Small tint differences show clearly on a floor viewed at a low angle. Keep a labeled quart for touch-ups.

Even with a day of grinder rental and prep supplies, a painted two-car garage usually comes in well below the cheapest two-part epoxy kit. For a full comparison against coatings, see our [epoxy garage floor cost](/epoxy-garage-floor-cost/) breakdown.

sections.h: Which Concrete Floor Paint Is Best for Each Room?

blocks.p: Use an epoxy-modified acrylic in the garage, a breathable acrylic in the basement, an acrylic enamel outdoors, a pro-grade acrylic in workshops and a slip-resistant coating on steps.
BEHR or Rust-Oleum one-part paint, etched or ground first, with the full vehicle cure observed. Set jack stands on plywood pads so they cannot punch through the film.

Moisture testing matters most here, because below-grade slabs pass vapor. Choose a breathable acrylic or epoxy-modified paint labeled for basements, skip alkyds, and run a dehumidifier while it cures; our picks for the [best dehumidifier for a basement](/best-dehumidifier-for-basement/) help keep humidity in check. If the walls are block, the [best paint for cinder block](/best-paint-for-cinder-block/) guide covers that side.
Outdoor slabs need UV-stable color, flexibility for freeze-thaw and grip when wet. Benjamin Moore Floor and Patio handles all three, with Sure Step on the steps.
Tread-Plex dries hard and fast under boots and carts. Paint walkway lines or a border in a safety color so traffic routes stand out.
Use Sure Step or Over Armor. Smooth gloss paint on a wet step is a genuine fall hazard.

sections.h: How Long Does Painted Concrete Last?

blocks.p: With good prep, one-part floor paint commonly lasts three to five years in a garage, five to seven in a basement or utility room, and two to four on an exposed patio, where UV and freeze-thaw cycles take a toll.
The slab, the traffic and the climate count for more than the brand. An etched, dry, fully cured floor lands at the top of the range; one painted over a sealer may not survive its first winter.

Sweep or dust-mop grit often, since sand acts like sandpaper underfoot. Mop with plain water or a pH-neutral cleaner and avoid harsh solvents. Wipe oil, brake fluid and gasoline promptly, and put felt pads under furniture legs.

blocks.h3: Add a maintenance coat before it fails

blocks.p: When traffic lanes look thin but the paint is still bonded, clean, scuff-sand those areas and roll one maintenance coat. Once paint peels in sheets, the floor needs stripping or grinding, which is several times the work.

blocks.h3: When a floor has outgrown paint

blocks.p: If you are repainting a garage every two years, step up to a two-part system or a penetrating sealer. Both cost more up front and often less over a decade.

mistakes: Painting over a sealer or curing compound

New slabs often carry a curing compound, and older floors have usually been sealed at some point. Paint bonds to that layer and peels off with it. If water beads anywhere on the floor, strip or grind the surface first, no matter what the can promises about adhesion.
Skipping the moisture test in a basement

Vapor rising through a below-grade slab pushes paint off from beneath and leaves blisters and white powder. A day under taped plastic shows the problem before you buy any paint. If droplets form, solve the moisture or use a product labeled for damp conditions.
Using interior wall paint on the floor

Wall paint is made for surfaces nobody walks on. On a floor it stays soft, scuffs under shoes and wears through within weeks. Floor enamels use harder resins made for abrasion and repeated mopping, and the small saving on wall paint costs you the whole job.
Rolling one thick coat to save time

A heavy coat stays soft underneath, traps moisture and is far more likely to wrinkle or peel. Floor paints are built for two thin coats. Roll until the film looks even and slightly translucent at the edges, then let it dry fully before the second coat.

Most floor paints handle foot traffic after a day but need about a week, longer in cool weather, before a car sits on them. Warm tires soften under-cured paint, grip it and pull it up when you back out. Park outside until the full label cure has passed.
bottomLine: For most garages, basements and patios, BEHR Premium 1-Part Epoxy is the concrete floor paint to start with: it rolls like latex, covers inside and outside slabs and tints to almost any color. Rust-Oleum's one-part paint gives a glossier garage floor, Tread-Plex is the tough choice for shops, Benjamin Moore Floor and Patio is the looker for living spaces, and Sure Step or Over Armor fixes slippery or worn concrete. Run the water drop, plastic sheet and tape tests first, etch or grind, roll two thin coats and wait out the full cure. If a car parks there daily, buy a two-part coating instead.

faqs.q: What is the best paint for concrete floors?
faqs.a: The best paint for concrete floors in most homes is an epoxy-modified acrylic such as BEHR Premium 1-Part Epoxy, which is harder than plain latex but still rolls on like ordinary paint. A premium acrylic enamel like Benjamin Moore Floor and Patio looks better in living spaces and outdoors, and a slip-resistant coating suits stairs and wet areas.

faqs.q: What is the best garage floor paint for concrete?
faqs.a: The best garage floor paint for concrete is an epoxy-modified acrylic such as BEHR Premium 1-Part Epoxy or Rust-Oleum EpoxyShield 1-Part, applied over an etched or ground slab and left to cure fully before parking. If a car parks on the floor every day and you want five years or more, a two-part epoxy kit is the better investment.

faqs.q: What is the most durable concrete floor paint?
faqs.a: The most durable concrete floor paints are epoxy-modified acrylics and pro-line acrylics such as Sherwin-Williams Tread-Plex, which resist scuffs and frequent cleaning better than plain latex enamel. Durability depends mostly on prep, though: an etched, dry, clean slab and two thin coats with a full cure matter more than the brand.

faqs.q: What is the best concrete floor paint for a basement?
faqs.a: The best concrete floor paint for a basement is a breathable acrylic or epoxy-modified acrylic labeled for basement floors, such as BEHR Premium 1-Part Epoxy. Run a plastic-sheet moisture test first, skip oil-based alkyds, and keep a dehumidifier running while the paint cures so the film hardens properly.

faqs.q: Do I need to etch concrete before painting it?
faqs.a: You need to etch concrete before painting if the surface is smooth, dense or beads water. Etching opens the pores so paint can grip. Older, porous slabs that absorb water within a minute may only need cleaning, while sealed or glassy floors usually need a diamond grind rather than an etch.

faqs.q: What is the best exterior concrete floor paint?
faqs.a: The best exterior concrete floor paint is an acrylic enamel rated for outdoor use, such as Benjamin Moore Floor and Patio or BEHR Premium 1-Part Epoxy, which handle UV and freeze-thaw better than interior products. Add a slip-resistant coating like INSL-X Sure Step on steps, and use KILZ Over Armor on rough, worn slabs.

faqs.q: How long does concrete floor paint last?
faqs.a: Concrete floor paint commonly lasts three to five years in a garage, five to seven years in a basement or utility room, and two to four years on an exposed patio. Proper etching, a dry slab, two thin coats and a full cure push it toward the top of those ranges.
